articles.title: AFA Urges Congress to Fully Fund Space Force, Ramp Up F-35 Procurement
articles.body:
The Air & Space Forces Association urged congressional leaders this week to fully fund the Space Force’s record-breaking $71.1 billion budget request for fiscal 2027, increase F-35 procurement, and finish revisions to troops’ Basic Allowance for Housing.
With six weeks to go before the end of the fiscal year and a looming midterm election, it is almost certain the Defense Department will start the new fiscal year Oct. 1 under a continuing resolution, freezing funding at the fiscal 2026 level and delaying new programs from getting started.
AFA President and CEO retired Lt. Gen. Burt Field and Chair of the Board Kathleen Ferguson addressed Speaker of House Rep. Mike Johnson (R-La.); House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.); Senate Majority Leader Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.); and Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in a letter detailing challenges ahead. Copies were sent copies to the top Republicans and Democrats on the Armed Services, Appropriations Committees,, and defense appropriations subcommittees in each chamber.
Both the House and Senate will return from recess in September with the state of play for 2027 funding in disarray. The Pentagon’s $1.5 trillion request split between two proposals: $1.15 trillion funded through the normal legislative process and $350 billion through reconciliation, a process that only requires a simple majority to clear the Senate, enabling the Republican majority to pass it on a party-line vote. House appropriators largely stuck to that $1.15 trillion request, but the reconciliation now in the works has been cut to $60 billion—mostly for priorities identified in the White House’s supplemental funding request, not the 2027 budget.
That has budget analysts and defense experts openly skeptical that Republicans will be able to push through the $350 billion originally proposed by the White House. Nor does anyone expect Congress to pass the $1.15 trillion regular budget on time. The House and Senate have already passed slightly different continuing resolutions funding the government at fiscal 2026 levels into December and must resolve their differences when they return from recess in September.
The potential impacts for the Air Force and Space Force are huge. More than 6 percent of the Air Force’s budget was supposed to come through reconciliation, and 17 percent of the Space Force’s. That money was meant to fund 14 of the 38 F-35A fighters the Air Force wanted to buy, a new constellation of airborne targeting satellites, and more than half of the construction funds for Air Force military family housing.
AFA’s letter doesn’t advocate for reconciliation or a particular funding approach—just the key priorities included in the Pentagon’s overall request.
“Congress cannot allow the uncertainty of the appropriations and reconciliation process to become a reason to underfund the capabilities and resources our Airmen, Guardians, and military families need,” said Field. “These investments in our Air Force and Space Force are too critical to let slip. Congress must act to ensure our military can meet the pace of threats we face.”
F-35A
The Air Force’s request of 38 F-35As in 2027 is up from 24 in fiscal 2026—but still well short of the 72 experts say is necessary to reverse declines in the Air Force fighter fleet.
AFA’s letter to Congress urges lawmakers to fund F-35A production “at the maximum executable rate possible … not less than 60 aircraft per year.”
To do that, lawmakers would have to add funds to the Pentagon’s request. If that’s not possible, the letter notes that “at an absolute minimum, Congress should provide the full discretionary and mandatory funding requested in the President’s Budget Request for 38 F-35As.”
It’s not just this year’s F-35 production that needs to be addressed, though—Congress is also considering granting the Pentagon authority to negotiate multiyear procurement of F-35s, an arrangement that could allow the military to lock in lower prices for more jets over time. AFA’s letter endorses this proposal, which would be included in the annual defense policy bill.
Space Force
The Space Force’s $71.1 budget proposal is by far the most ambitious in the service’s short history: more than double its 2026 funding. It includes $5 billion for the Resilient Missile Warning and Tracking program, $7 billion for airborne targeting satellites, $1 billion for ground targeting satellites, $4 billion for 22 National Security Space Launch missions, and $1 billion for four new operations centers.
Almost half of the procurement funding in that request was supposed to come through reconciliation, particularly the airborne moving target indicator program—so the uncertainty on Capitol Hill threatens huge portions of the Space Force’s plans.
“As Congress determines whether to provide these resources through regular appropriations, reconciliation, or a combination of the two, there is a significant risk that essential Space Force funding could be omitted, fragmented, or delayed,” AFA’s letter states.
AFA’s leaders urged Congress to fully fund the $71.1 billion topline “regardless of the legislative vehicle used to provide it.”
“The Space Force cannot afford delays in fielding the capabilities and infrastructure Guardians need to deter—and, if necessary, defeat—growing threats in space,” the letter states.
Housing
Among several service member quality of life issues highlighted in the letter, AFA leaders made a particular case for Congress to use its defense budget and policy bills to finish reforms started to the Basic Allowance for Housing, the money given to troops to pay for housing depending on their home station, experience, and number of dependents.
Advocates say BAH can change wildly year to year, is not always aligned with expensive areas where troops are stationed, and the methodology for determining the allowance is outdated.
“AFA urges the Department to complete this work expeditiously and Congress to act on its findings to ensure BAH more accurately reflects the real cost of adequate housing in local markets,” AFA leaders wrote.

articles.title: Russian and Egyptian nuclear authorities reject ‘biased’ Politico report
articles.body:
Russian and Egyptian nuclear authorities reject ‘biased’ Politico report
 Russia and Egypt have strongly challenged a report by Politico alleging violations at the El Daba nuclear power project (NPP). The report which the Axel Springer-owned outlet admits is sourced from an intelligence official is “biased,” they have claimed, insisting that the venture fully complies with international safety standards.
El Dabaa, Egypt’s first nuclear power plant, is being built by Russian state corporation Rosatom in Matrouh Governorate. Launched in 2017, the $28.75 billion development comprises four VVER-1200 Generation III+ reactors and is jointly financed by Moscow and Cairo, with Russia covering about 85% through a 22-year loan. Construction is expected to be completed by 2029, and the plant to come online by 2030. When fully operational, the plant is expected to meet roughly 10% of Egypt’s electricity needs, while freeing up millions of cubic meters of natural gas for domestic use or export.
Politico’s claims
Politico on Monday published a lengthy report detailing purported violations at the site.
According to the outlet, the letter was part of a tranche it obtained through an intelligence official that also included confidential Rosatom documents outlining violations identified in the company’s own reviews and audits.
Citing a “confidential letter” from an unknown party addressed to an unnamed Rosatom executive, it claimed that Egypt’s Nuclear Power Plants Authority (NPPA) – the government agency responsible for the country’s civilian nuclear power stations – had identified “defects” at reactor units, violations of “nuclear safety culture,” and “deliberate negligence” by a project official.
The document also reportedly details construction delays, security breaches, unprofessional conduct, and an attempt to conceal a serious accident.
How have Russia and Egypt’s nuclear agencies reacted to Politico’s claims?
Rosatom was the first to reject the allegations.
“None of the claims made in the Politico report have been substantiated through the contractual, technical, or regulatory procedures established for the project,” Rosatom’s press service told RBK. The company said that El Dabaa is being implemented under Russian-Egyptian intergovernmental agreements and a contract with the NPPA, with all work subject to continuous regulatory oversight.
The Egyptian nuclear authority later issued its own statement, saying that the report “presented an inaccurate and unbalanced picture” and drew conclusions without proper technical and regulatory context. It added that it had received a request for comment before publication but considered the article too politicized to “warrant a response.”
El Dabaa meets the “highest internationally recognized nuclear safety and security standards,” the NPPA insisted, dismissing issues outlined by the outlet as “typical” for a project of this scale.
Politico is attempting to draw El Dabaa “into a broader narrative aimed at serving other political objectives,” the NPPA claimed.
“Following a careful review of the article, it became clear that it lacked the required balance and objectivity and contained inaccuracies and reflected a biased approach.”
How did Politico structure its PR offensive?
Politico framed the purported violations at El Dabaa as posing broader risks to cooperation with Russia on peaceful nuclear energy, pointed to Rosatom’s Paks II project in Hungary, which generates half of Hungary’s electricity but which has repeatedly fueled tensions between Budapest and Brussels.
The El Dabaa allegations “cast a shadow over the Paks II project” and could “reinforce concerns” in Brussels, where Politico Europe has a sizeable and influential newsroom, about entrusting critical European infrastructure to a Russian company.
Politico also cited the Royal United Services Institute, a UK-based think tank co-funded by the British government, the US State Department and the European Commission, which last month urged Western countries against doing business with Rosatom. Politico then released a supporting article citing Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sybiga, who seized on the outlet’s “investigation” to call for EU sanctions on Rosatom and an end to nuclear energy cooperation with Moscow.
Western pressure on Rosatom
Rosatom controls nearly half of global uranium enrichment capacity and supplies nuclear fuel to reactors worldwide. Its critical global role and expertise have allowed it to avoid sweeping Western sanctions imposed on much of Russia’s energy sector since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022. However, some subsidiaries, executives, and projects face targeted restrictions.
Several European countries and the US have historically relied on Russian nuclear fuel and enrichment services, making a comprehensive ban economically costly.
While Washington banned Russian uranium imports in 2024, it introduced waivers allowing purchases until the full ban takes effect in 2028. Kiev, however, has pressed the EU and G7 for sweeping sanctions on Rosatom, particularly over its operation of the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), Europe’s largest nuclear facility. Russia took control of the plant in March 2022, and the facility and nearby Energodar have been repeatedly targeted by Ukrainian artillery and drones since.
Russia has long argued that Western sanctions, particularly on energy, are illegal and self-defeating. Rosatom CEO Aleksey Likhachev acknowledged in May that restrictions have hampered its overseas projects, particularly by complicating international payments, but said that they have ultimately strengthened the company’s technological independence by encouraging closer cooperation with Russian manufacturers and new suppliers.
Who owns Politico – and do they have an agenda?
Politico is owned by Axel Springer SE, the German media conglomerate that acquired the outlet from founder Robert Allbritton in October 2021.
Axel Springer operates under binding corporate principles known as “The Essentials,” which explicitly champion free markets, Israel, and US-EU transatlantic relationship. While Russia and Ukraine are not named, the company’s leadership has presented its staunch support for Kiev as an extension of its commitments to defending democracy against authoritarianism and strengthening transatlantic ties.
That openly prescribed ideological framework has raised questions about editorial independence, with critics and staff questioning whether mandatory corporate values can coexist with newsroom impartiality. CEO Mathias Döpfner has publicly defended the principles as fundamental to Axel Springer and told employees who reject them that they are free to leave.
Axel Springer’s Cold War history is also noteworthy. In the 1990s, investigative journalist Murray Waas cited former US intelligence officials alleging that the German media mogul received roughly $7 million in covert CIA funding in the 1950s – around $97 million in today’s money. The funds were reportedly intended to promote pro-American, anti-communist sentiment in postwar West Germany and support Springer’s expanding media operation, which would include right-leaning, pro-Western publications such as Bild.

articles.title: US left with few good options as Iran war strategy falters
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US left with few good options as Iran war strategy falters
The United States is running out of options for ending its war with Iran after the 60-day memorandum of understanding expired on Monday without producing an agreement, according to military experts.
Almost six months into the conflict, Washington has failed to force Tehran to accept its demands through military pressure, while the prospect of a ground invasion remains strategically problematic and deeply unpopular among US voters.
That leaves the administration confronting a series of difficult choices to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, ranging from renewed military attacks, a ground offensive in the south, accepting a deal that leaves Iran partially in control of the waterway or walking away without an agreement.
"The United States' military options have diminished further over the past few months,” Jason Campbell, a former US Pentagon official, told The New Arab.
He pointed to the deteriorating condition of US aircraft carriers as well as damage inflicted by Iranian attacks on American military bases in the region.
"The strikes that hit the air base in Jordan with a high degree of accuracy demonstrate the extent of Iran's ability to target US positions," Campbell said, adding that Tehran's ability to put American troops at risk "also limits Washington's options when it comes to a potential ground offensive".
'Strategic defeat'
Campbell argued that the Trump administration is reluctant to acknowledge a more fundamental problem: that the US has already suffered a strategic setback.
"The administration does not appear prepared to formally accept what I think has been clear for several months, which is that this war was a strategic defeat for the United States," he said.
Washington instead appears to be buying time by maintaining its naval blockade in the hope that economic pressure will eventually force Tehran to accept its demands.
This, too, carries risks.
"There is an assumption that we can continue doing this without cost," Campbell said, warning that Iran could decide it would no longer allow Washington to dictate the pace of events and instead seek to impose a political or military price on the White House for maintaining the status quo.
An Iranian official threatened to do exactly that on Monday, handing the US an ultimatum to negotiate a deal in the coming weeks or face renewed attacks.
Political damage
Campbell said Tehran appeared determined not only to inflict material costs on the US but to damage Trump politically ahead of the midterm elections in November.
Iranian statements, he said, suggested Tehran could be prepared to remain in confrontation with Washington for the remainder of Trump's presidency.
Nate Swanson, director of the Atlantic Council's Iran Strategy Project, was similarly downbeat on Trump's options.
Speaking to The New York Times, Swanson said Trump's threat on Monday to "bomb the shit out of" Oman reflected his frustration with a predicament of his own making.
"He’s just reflexively lashing out, and this time Oman got in the crosshairs," he said.
Trump could continue an economic pressure campaign that has so far failed to achieve its objectives, escalate military operations despite dwindling US ammunition stocks, or return to negotiations and accept an agreement resembling previous diplomatic arrangements, Swanson said.
US officials have indicated they will return to economic pressure in the coming weeks, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowing to impose measures that "have never been seen in the history of economic isolation".
Another possibility would be for Washington to step back from the Strait of Hormuz and demand that its Gulf allies assume greater responsibility for securing the waterway.
"I’m wondering if at some point, either by choice or incompetence, we kind of just put our blinders on and let the Gulf figure it out," Swanson said.
Justin Logan, director of defence and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute, said Washington's fundamental problem is that it is now fighting to fix problems created by the war, such as re-opening the Strait of Hormuz.
"The tragic part here is that the United States is clawing to try to get back to the state of the Middle East before the war started," he told The New York Times.

articles.title: Israeli strikes hit airbase runway in northwest Syria but no casualties, state TV reports
articles.body:
Israel strikes an air base in northwest Syria to prevent Turkish troops from deploying
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — Israel struck an air base in northwest Syria early Tuesday, saying it aimed to prevent Turkish troops from deploying there.
Turkey, which has close ties with the Syrian government and has been providing assistance to Syria’s military, has tense relations with Israel. The rival countries have sought to curb each other’s influence in neighboring Syria.
Eight strikes hit the runway of the Abu Duhur air base in the northwestern province of Idlib, causing damage but no casualties, state TV said. Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told reporters in Damascus that Syria condemns the “Israeli aggression,” adding that the strikes were “an unjustified provocation, a violation of Syria’s sovereignty, and a direct threat to regional and global stability.”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said in a statement that Israel had attacked the base because Syria had been “on the verge of breaching” an agreed-upon “status quo in security matters” by allowing Turkish troops to deploy there.
“Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel’s security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings,” the statement said.
The Foreign Ministry of Turkey condemned the attack in a statement and called for “the international community to take a more decisive stance to end Israel’s escalating aggression against Syria and to ensure accountability for these actions that disregard international law.”
The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a war monitor, said foreign fighters used to stay at the base before they were recently asked to leave. The Observatory added that Turkey, which is a main backer of Syria’s government, has been rehabilitating the air base that had been out of service for years during Syria’s conflict that left nearly half a million people dead.
Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria, posted on X that Washington is “deeply concerned that the confirmed Israeli airstrikes” on the Abu Duhur air base constitute “an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability.”
The government of Syria’s Interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa has neither “adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces” but has repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel, Barrack said.
The United States has in the past hosted, and will continue in the future to host, discussions to encourage diplomacy, Barrack added.
Regional countries including Qatar, Egypt and Saudi Arabia also issued statements condemning the strikes.
Since the fall of Bashar Assad’s government in December 2024 when insurgents marched into his seat of power in Damascus, tensions between Israel and Turkey over Syria have been on the rise.
Israel carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after Assad’s fall, mainly destroying assets of the Syrian army to keep them out of the hands of his successors. The Israeli military also seized control of a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone in southern Syria, which it continues to occupy.
Israeli drone strikes on a southern suburb of Damascus last year killed eight soldiers and wounded others.
The new authorities in Damascus have said they do not want a conflict with Israel, but Israel has remained suspicious of the government led by former Islamist insurgents.
U.S.-mediated talks between Israel and Syria aimed at reaching a security agreement have been ongoing for more than a year but have so far failed to produce a deal.
——
Associated Press writer Suzan Fraser in Ankara contributed.

articles.title: Iraq arrests senior PMF figure amid disarmament push
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq arrests senior PMF intelligence official amid disarmament push
Iraqi security forces have detained a senior commander in the Iran-aligned Harakat al-Nujaba group, in a move that could intensify tensions between the government and armed factions resisting efforts to bring weapons under state control.
Abbas Hussein al-Yaqoubi, a senior Nujaba figure who also serves as an intelligence official within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), was detained on Monday in the southern province of Dhi Qar, according to Iraqi officials and security sources.
Security sources in Baghdad told The New Arab that a special unit linked to Iraq's Counter Terrorism Service raided a residential building about 360 kilometres south of Baghdad and detained Yaqoubi.
Helicopters and armoured vehicles accompanied the force during the operation, according to one security source. The unit subsequently left Dhi Qar for Baghdad without clashes.
The Iraqi News Agency also reported Yaqoubi's detention, identifying him as the intelligence chief for Harakat al-Nujaba and an intelligence director for the PMF's Baghdad Belt Operations Command.
The PMF, however, said Yaqoubi had voluntarily surrendered to the authorities.
No official reason for the arrest was immediately disclosed.
But a former Iraqi lawmaker from the Fatah Alliance told The New Arab that the detention was linked to investigations into drone attacks carried out in recent months. He provided no further details.
Yaqoubi has also been accused of involvement in attacks targeting US forces in Iraq.
Platforms affiliated with Iraqi armed factions described the detention as a "kidnapping" and called for demonstrations in the Fadhiliya area of Nasiriyah, the capital of Dhi Qar province.
Pressure over militia weapons
The arrest comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Iraq's government as a late-September deadline approaches for bringing weapons under state control.
Several armed factions linked to the PMF have categorically rejected surrendering their weapons while US forces remain in Iraq, raising the prospect of a confrontation with the government.
Harakat al-Nujaba, led by Akram al-Kaabi, is among Iraq's most powerful Iran-aligned armed factions. The United States has designated the group a terrorist organisation.
The detention could become an early test of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's willingness and ability to confront factions refusing to comply with the government's disarmament push.
Othman al-Shaibani, a member of the Iraqi parliament's Security and Defence Committee, recently described warnings issued by Zaidi over the weapons issue as "extremely serious".
In a televised interview, Shaibani said the prime minister had warned that if Iraqi institutions failed to disarm armed groups themselves, outside powers, particularly the United States, could take matters into their own hands.
"Zaidi clearly warned that if national institutions are unable to carry out their duties in disarming the factions, the international community, particularly the American side, will undertake the task itself," Shaibani said.
Such intervention would not necessarily be limited to political pressure, he added, warning that it could escalate to strikes and targeted killings against faction positions.
The government, Shaibani noted, was seeking to avoid such a scenario by resolving the issue domestically and bringing armed groups under state authority.
'Last chance' before 30 September
According to Shaibani, Zaidi has warned that failure to address the armed factions could expose Iraq to international isolation and severe economic consequences, potentially including restrictions on financial transfers and the flow of oil revenues.
Such measures could ultimately affect Baghdad's ability to meet its financial obligations and pay public-sector salaries, he said.
Shaibani also claimed the prime minister had warned of the possibility of renewed international oversight of Iraq and a return to measures associated with Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, which he said would undermine the country's sovereignty.
The government views 30 September as a "last chance" to avoid those consequences, according to Shaibani.
He said Zaidi had expressed a willingness to confront any group refusing to surrender its weapons and viewed bringing arms under state control as non-negotiable, "whatever the cost, even his life".
Yaqoubi's detention could bring that confrontation closer.
With some of Iraq's most powerful armed factions insisting they will not disarm as long as American troops remain in the country, the arrest of a senior Nujaba figure risks becoming more than an isolated security operation, and instead an early indication of how far Baghdad is prepared to go to enforce its deadline.

articles.title: ‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments
articles.body:
To many observers they will appear dehumanising and offensive. To many Ukrainians, however, they are a brutal reminder of the fate that awaits Russian soldiers who take part in Vladimir Putin’s invasion, as well as a potent propaganda weapon.
Over the past year and a half, videos of kamikaze drones chasing Russian service personnel to their deaths have become a distinctive genre on social media. They are the brainchild of Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces and founder of “Magyar’s Birds”, named after his call sign.
Brovdi’s 414th aviation strike brigade has pioneered the use of battlefield video, much of it recorded by first-person-view drones. The death videos are known as yoblyks, a portmanteau that combines the root of the Ukrainian for “fuck” with an affectionate diminutive form. The closest English translation is probably “fuckling”.
Early each morning, a military editor known by his call sign Catman sifts through battlefield clips recorded the previous day, selecting some for a two-minute compilation and adding pulsing or mystical music. A longer online reel is titled “Yoblyks of the Week”.
Defending his work, Catman said the videos played an important role in demoralising ordinary Russians and revealing the true cost of the Kremlin’s unprovoked war. “My goal is to show Russians that if they mobilise in Ukraine they will be killed, that it’s a one-way ticket and death is waiting for them,” he said.
He acknowledged that the clips were deliberately arranged to mock the victims, who are sometimes seen throwing sticks at the drones to try to knock them off course, or falling over as they run. Though the moment of death is not shown, the last frame is a closeup of a soldier’s face.
“We have a phrase: laughter kills fear. Our main task is to laugh at these enemies and to depict them as helpless. This boosts the morale of our forces,” he said. “It’s impossible for me to feel sorry for them. It’s war, after all, not a movie.”
Typically, the Russian soldiers are killed while walking or travelling by motorbike to the frontline. Some are unaware they are at risk from drones, Catman said, and appear to have been tricked by their commanders. “Their training is short. A lot die just two weeks after enlisting,” he said.
He described most of the soldiers as “banal donkey men” ordered to carry provisions or fuel to exposed Russian positions. Others drag communication cables. Since February, when Elon Musk shut down his satellite internet service Starlink in Russia, officers in the rear have struggled to contact frontline units.
Another member of Magyar’s Birds said there was compelling evidence the Russians were routinely misled about dangers. “You can see from the videos a lot of them are not even hiding,” he said. “They use their radio sets. A large number are fooled by the lie that everything will be OK, that they are going to their positions and are totally safe.”
The brigade has an archive of about 3,600 videos. Only two feature women, both wearing combat uniform and carrying assault rifles. “There is no difference for me. They are all enemies,” Catman said.
The videos play an important part in verifying Russian losses, which are running at more than 30,000 soldiers a month killed or injured, according to Kyiv.
Brovdi said he had no qualms about publishing material that many in the west might find distasteful and morally dubious. “God forbid they should ever experience pain. Because those of us in Ukraine who have experienced real physical pain from war would never agree with that perspective,” he said.
In daily posts, Brovdi uses language that some might find gratuitous, for instance describing Russians as “worms” pecked by “birds”.
He said: “When the war started, everything changed. There was a desire to humiliate the enemy as much as possible, not with typical words but exotic ones. It was only natural that military technical folklore and coinages such as ‘yoblyk’ found their way into my speech. They existed before AI.”
The videos have sparked several trolling subgenres. Some Russian women post photos of themselves saying farewell to their husbands as they leave to take part in what Putin calls a “special military operation”. Ukrainians identify the men and subsequently reply with drone footage showing their deaths.
According to Catman, the yoblyks have a wide audience, including inside Russia. “There is very little information there about soldiers who go missing. Some people search and take screenshots. Mothers or wives then post messages saying something bad has happened to their loved ones,” he said.
Pro-war Russian bloggers post images on Telegram channels of Ukrainian soldiers dying in battle. Other videos show the killing of unarmed Ukrainian prisoners of war – a crime. The Russian internet includes AI-generated fakes that purport to show Ukrainian military personnel criticising their army leadership.
Anatolii Loza, a Ukrainian volunteer who was captured and imprisoned by Russia and recently swapped, said he saw nothing wrong with yoblyks. “International law doesn’t apply to killing combatants on the field of battle,” he said. “The Russians come to shoot our soldiers and civilians. They are wearing uniform. They deserve their fate.”
Loza’s wife, Olena, said attitudes inside Ukraine hardened after spring 2022, when Russian forces killed hundreds of civilians in the cities of Bucha and Mariupol, leaving their bodies on the streets. Of yoblyks, she said: “I don’t find these videos informative. I’m already furious with Russia.”
At the HQ of Magyar’s Birds, Catman said black humour was essential during wartime. “It’s important for our own people to say we are not just surviving. We need to show we are flourishing and hitting back hard against the enemy.”
- 
  Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest, by Luke Harding, is published on 27 August by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

articles.title: Iranian lawmaker says Tehran would respond in kind if US used nuclear weapon
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
An Iranian lawmaker said Tehran would respond in kind if the US used a nuclear weapon against Iran, commenting on a media report about the possibility of such an attack, according to local media on Wednesday.
Fada Hossein Maleki, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, made the remarks in an interview with Iranian news outlet Khabar Online.
Asked how likely he considered a US nuclear attack on Iran, Maleki said: “I do not rule out an ill-considered action by (US President Donald) Trump, but I do not think he would dare to do such a thing, because such an action could plunge the world into a dangerous war.”
“If such an action is taken, the Islamic Republic of Iran will also respond, and its reaction will be proportionate to the type of weapon used against Iran,” he added.
Pressed on whether this meant Iran would use a nuclear weapon if the US attacked Iran with one, Maleki replied: “Whatever the US uses, Iran will respond to it.”
Maleki did not explicitly say that Iran possesses nuclear weapons.
The lawmaker also warned Washington against further military action, saying Iran has “multiple options” at its disposal and that any US move could draw a response “at the same level or even beyond.”
“Many of Iran’s weapons and military capabilities have not yet been unveiled,” Maleki said, arguing that Tehran has moved from a defensive posture to what he described as “active and offensive deterrence.”
Turning to stalled Tehran-Washington talks, Maleki accused Trump of failing to honor commitments under the memorandum of understanding between the two sides.
He said Iran would not return to negotiations unless Washington abides by its previous commitments, adding that issues including the Strait of Hormuz would remain unresolved otherwise.
Maleki said Iran’s talks with Oman are a separate bilateral track, adding that Tehran rejected US participation in those discussions.
Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June under Pakistani mediation aimed at ending their war and paving the way for negotiations on a final agreement.
Talks have since stalled amid disputes over the implementation of the memorandum, including issues related to the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest tensions follow months of hostilities since the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against US and Israeli targets and US assets across the region.

articles.title: Pentagon eyes smaller US military presence in Gulf after Iran war: Report
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
The Pentagon is reassessing its military footprint in the Middle East, signaling that the Iran war could potentially reshape the US presence in the region, The Washington Post reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
According to the report, Pentagon is considering whether to reduce troops in the Gulf, where major US bases have suffered months of Iranian strikes.
The damage has created a rare opportunity to reconsider the US military posture in the region, the report said, with officials indicating that some bases may not be rebuilt in their previous form.
The review is being led by the Pentagon’s policy office, while the Joint Staff and US Central Command are also examining the issue, according to the report.
A senior Pentagon official said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had not ordered a formal review, describing the effort instead as “prudent planning” that could help guide decisions on rebuilding damaged bases.
“Decisions are going to have to be made on some of this stuff,” the official said.
US Central Command typically maintains about 40,000 troops at nearly 20 sites stretching from Jordan to Oman. Since early this year, Washington has deployed additional warships, fighter aircraft and air defense systems to the region and carried out more than 13,000 strikes against Iran.
The largest permanent US bases in the region are concentrated in the Gulf, including the Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and major Army and Air Force facilities in countries such as Kuwait.

articles.title: Update: UAE says halts trade with Iran after detecting 2 ballistic missiles
articles.body:
DUBAI, Aug. 19 (Xinhua) -- The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran until further notice, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs said early Wednesday, a few hours after the country said it detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, Afra Al Hameli, the director of the foreign ministry's strategic communications department, said the decision came in light of regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security.
The statement reiterated the UAE's commitment to dialogue, cooperation and regional integration as essential means of advancing peace, stability and prosperity in the region.
Earlier in the day, the UAE's Ministry of Defense said its air defense systems detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran toward the country, adding that the missiles were targeting maritime traffic.
The ministry said that the first missile fell outside the UAE's territorial waters, while the second fell within the country's territorial waters.
So far, no casualties or damage have been reported in connection with the missiles. ■

articles.title: Danish conscripts deployed to Greenland amid Trump threats
articles.body:
Danish conscripts deployed to Greenland amid Trump threats
Denmark has deployed a batch of fresh military conscripts to Greenland for the first time in modern history, as Copenhagen seeks to assert its control over the Arctic territory in response to threats of annexation from US President Donald Trump.
Around 100 conscripts from the Schleswig Infantry Regiment arrived in Nuuk in early August, Denmark’s military said in a press release on Tuesday. The group will divide their time between training and “operational tasks,” the military explained, with some troops stationed in Nuuk and others sent 350km north to Kangerlussuaq, an airbase used by US forces throughout the Second World War and Cold War.
The conscripts deployed to Greenland are the first batch of recruits to serve 11-month stints in the Danish military. In 2024, Denmark extended conscription from four months to 11, broadened the draft to include women, and ordered annual conscription numbers to increase from 5,000 to 7,000.
The military’s press release framed the deployment as an opportunity for recruits to “practice and train military skills in unfamiliar terrain.” The statement made no mention of Denmark’s ongoing dispute with the US over Greenland, but it did note that the conscripts will take part in Operation Arctic Endurance – a military exercise launched in direct response to Trump’s threats to annex the territory.
Trump started threatening to annex Greenland last year, claiming that the US needs the landmass “for the purpose of national security” – namely to host elements of his promised ‘Golden Dome’ ballistic missile defense network. Trump has also said that he wants “Greenland for its rare-earth minerals.”
Denmark launched the exercise in January, after Trump and other top US officials refused to rule out the use of military force to annex Greenland. Two weeks before the operation was announced, Trump joked that Denmark’s entire military presence on Greenland amounted to “two dog sleds.”
Eleven other NATO states have sent troops to take part in the exercise, including France, Germany, and the UK. Operation Arctic Endurance is a small-scale exercise, with fewer than 300 Danish and allied troops in Greenland at any one time before the arrival of the conscripts.
Copenhagen viewed an armed conflict with the US as highly unlikely, government and military sources told Denmark’s DR broadcaster in March, but placed troops in Greenland as an insurance policy. By stationing troops on Greenland “with as many different flags on their shoulders as possible,” DR explained, the Danish government ensured that “the Americans would be forced to take a major hostile action if Donald Trump actually wanted to occupy Greenland militarily.”
“The cost to the US would be raised. The US would have to carry out a hostile act to get Greenland,” a defense source told the broadcaster.
As an American oil company moved drilling equipment onto Greenland last month, Trump posted an image of himself looming over Greenland on his Truth Social platform, along with the caption “Hello, Greenland!”

articles.title: Pentagon orders audit of 30 universities’ partnerships with foreign institutions
articles.body:
Pentagon orders audit of 30 universities’ partnerships with foreign institutions
The Department of Defense has ordered 30 U.S. universities to audit their partnerships with mostly Chinese universities and military training institutions as the Trump administration scrutinizes the country’s growing global influence.
If the schools don’t complete a review and terminate any arrangements deemed problematic within the next two weeks, they face losing funding. The goal is to protect taxpayer-funded research from theft and exploitation, the Pentagon said Monday.
“The Department of War has zero tolerance for academic partnerships that compromise our national security,” Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, said in a news release.
The release didn’t name the schools, but a U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters said they include Harvard University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Johns Hopkins University.
The schools didn’t immediately respond to emails from The Associated Press seeking comment.
Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, raised concerns that the announcement suggests, without any evidence, that the schools are engaged in wrongdoing.
The order comes after the Pentagon last month released an updated list of 130 foreign institutions it accused of engaging in “activities that increase the likelihood of U.S. government-funded research and development efforts being misappropriated.”
While the vast majority were Chinese, such as the University of Science and Technology of China and the country’s Academy of Military Medical Sciences, several Iranian and Russian institutions also appeared on the list.
The first version of the list was developed during Trump’s first term, with the help of the American Council on Education, Spreitzer said.
She said most of the council’s member institutions moved away from research partnerships with those institutions in the years that followed. She said she worries U.S. schools will be held liable for partnerships that predate the creation of the list.
“We don’t appreciate the implication that we are not good partners on research security, given that we helped create this list, and given that we’ve always partnered with the federal government when there has been national security concerns,” she said.
The audit comes as the Trump administration continues to express deep concern about China’s activities in the Americas, pushing back on Chinese ownership of ports at either end of the Panama Canal, infrastructure projects funded by China’s Belt and Road initiative in the region and Chinese investment in the telecommunications sector.
The Justice Department also is investigating whether Harvard University is allowing Chinese donors to create scholarships that exclude American students, adding to the barrage of federal inquiries the Trump administration has opened in its battle against the Ivy League school.
A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy said in a statement that the country opposes what it described as the politicization of “normal scientific, educational, and academic exchanges.”
“The U.S. side,” the statement continued, “should abandon the Cold War mentality and foster an open, fair, and non-discriminatory environment for educational, scientific, and people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States.” ___
Associated Press writer Collin Binkley contributed to this report.

articles.title: In cutting joint drills, Trump has given South Korea’s president what he wants. So why does Seoul look so uneasy?
articles.body:
At their first summit, in August last year, the South Korean president, Lee Jae Myung, told Donald Trump: “If you, Mr President, become the peacemaker, then I will assist you as the pacemaker.”
The remark at the Oval Office captured the thrust of Lee’s approach to North Korea: dial down the military posturing and make repeated peace overtures to revive dialogue, even if they have been consistently rejected by Pyongyang largely over Seoul’s insistence on denuclearisation.
Fast forward to this week, and Trump’s move to cut joint military exercises with South Korea echoes what Lee had himself floated, on several occasions, as a possible tool for drawing Pyongyang back to the table.
Lee’s broader message is that South Korea should take more responsibility for its own defence and reduce its reliance on others. On Tuesday, he used the moment to renew calls for wartime operational control of the military and progress on his country’s nuclear submarine programme.
Trump has delivered on the drills, albeit in the blunt, discourteous fashion typical of the president: via social media, hours before the drills were to begin.
Yet the move has inverted South Korea’s usual political lines, where the left-right divide is shaped more by attitudes toward North Korea – hawks v doves, confrontation v engagement – than by economic or social values.
Reducing joint drills has long been advocated by some on the Korean left. A rightwing US president imposing the policy on his centre-left South Korean counterpart lands awkwardly for both sides.
While some see the reduction as potentially useful for diplomacy, the louder concern in Seoul is that Trump is weakening a key pillar of deterrence, and leaving South Korea with little say over decisions that directly affect its security. That may strain an alliance that has been the bedrock of security on the peninsula since the Korean war.
The opposition conservative People Power party has called the decision a “security disaster” and warned of a return to “Korea passing”, a term used when Seoul feels sidelined in matters directly affecting it. Conservative newspapers have been almost unanimous in calling the cut reckless. The influential Chosun Ilbo has gone further, blaming Lee’s government directly for inviting it.
The left has not shared that sense of alarm. Hankyoreh, one of the country’s main progressive papers, raised no objection to the substance of Trump’s decision, only to how it was delivered: unilaterally and disrespectfully on social media, calling it “regrettable”. Kyunghyang Shinmun took a more positive view, saying the cut could help create an atmosphere for dialogue with North Korea, so long as deterrence held.
Reducing tensions with North Korea and creating space for dialogue are central to Lee’s agenda. The ruling party has been quiet on the move, but openly welcoming Trump’s decision could put it at odds with a base that has generally viewed Trump with suspicion, if not hostility.
Aside from the domestic politics, the episode is likely to deepen doubts about Washington’s commitment to its allies, doubts that have been building for years since Trump’s first term, said Prof Jaechun Kim, who teaches international relations at Sogang University, in Seoul.
Trust, he argued, is the foundation of any alliance, and remarks like Trump’s reinforce the impression that the US’s obligations are increasingly viewed “through a highly transactional lens”, one that could shape how South Koreans judge US reliability long after Trump has left office.
Then there is the issue of the nuclear deterrent. South Korea enjoys protection under the US nuclear umbrella, but public support for an independent deterrent among South Koreans and their neighbours has hovered around or above 70% in recent surveys. The latest news may push that support higher still.
Kim said he expects Pyongyang to welcome any sign of friction within the alliance but doubts that it views improving relations with Washington as a priority, given the stronger backing it now enjoys from China and Russia compared with during Trump’s first term.
“The irony,” he said, “is that [US] policies intended to reduce American burdens may ultimately strengthen calls for independent nuclear deterrents among US allies.”

articles.title: U.S. envoy warns Syria strike risked Israel-Türkiye clash
articles.body:
Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in northwestern Syria’s Idlib province early Tuesday with eight airstrikes, an attack U.S. Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack said carried real risk of triggering direct military confrontation between Israel, Türkiye and Syria.
“The Turkish forces did not know that Israeli aircraft were making their way to this specific Syrian base, nor did they know what their objective was, and therefore they might have decided to scramble fighter jets under the belief that they themselves were under attack,” Barrack told i24NEWS.
“Yesterday’s events were serious and concerning,” Barrack said. “Nevertheless, we are relieved that no lives were lost and that the situation did not escalate.”
Syrian state television reported the strikes hit the base’s runway and storage facilities, causing material damage but no casualties. The base sits about 70 kilometers (43 miles) from the Turkish border and had been out of service as a dedicated military airfield since 2013. Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Syria’s new government had been using it as a training center for its rebuilding armed forces.
The strike came shortly after a Turkish military delegation inspected the base as part of an effort to rehabilitate it, according to Syrian and Turkish reporting. Israel initially declined to comment, and Israeli military censors blocked reporting confirming the country’s involvement before Barrack named Israel publicly on X. Israel later acknowledged responsibility, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office saying Israel and Syria had “agreed to a status quo in security matters” that Damascus was “on the verge of breaching” by allowing Turkish forces to deploy at the base.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as a violation of Syria’s territorial integrity, and Syria’s Foreign Ministry called them “unjustified aggression.” Jordan also condemned the attack. The strike was the first Israeli attack on Syrian government military assets since March, according to i24NEWS.
Israel has struck Syrian sites near planned Turkish military inspections before. In March 2025, Israeli aircraft hit Syria’s T4 and Palmyra airbases hours before a Turkish delegation was due to arrive at those sites, a strike Israel publicly acknowledged at the time. Israel later struck T4 again in early April 2025. Those earlier strikes were driven by Israeli concern that Türkiye could deploy air defense systems and drones at T4, which would have expanded Ankara’s control over Syrian airspace and constrained Israeli operations there. The dispute over T4 led Israel and Türkiye to establish a military communication channel in 2025 aimed at preventing miscalculation.

articles.title: Israel strikes NE. Syria's abandoned Abu al-Duhur air base
articles.body:
Israel carried out a series of airstrikes on northeastern Syria's Abu al-Duhur military air base Tuesday, according to Syrian state media and a war monitor.
The attack on the disused air base came after a recent visit to the site by a Turkish delegation.
Israel has been carrying out incursions into Syrian territory since the December 2024 overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar Assad, including sending troops into a U.N.-patrolled buffer zone that separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights since 1974.
It has also hit key military sites including several airfields, according to the U.K.-based war monitor, Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.
"Israeli occupation aircraft early this morning targeted the runway ... with eight strikes," Syrian state television quoted an unidentified military source as saying.
It added that "the attack resulted in material damage to the airport's infrastructure, without causing casualties."
The facility has been out of service since 2012 and is currently protected by Syrian Defense Ministry forces, a security source told Agence France-Presse (AFP), without reporting any casualties.
According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the strikes came after "a visit by a Turkish military delegation to the airfield in recent days as part of efforts to reactivate it."
Türkiye is a key ally of the new government in Damascus.
No side has claimed the strikes on the airfield and the Israeli military said "no comment" in response to an AFP inquiry about the strikes.
A U.S.-led international coalition against the Daesh terrorist group has previously carried out strikes on senior terrorist figures in the northwest.
Syria is now part of the coalition.
Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since the fall of Assad and Israeli officials have said they intend to keep forces in a "security zone" in southern Syria, where they seek a broader so-called "demilitarized zone."
Damascus has repeatedly condemned incursions in the country's south.
During a joint press conference with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron in Damascus last month, Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa called for an "active French role" to halt Israeli escalations in his country.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also last month condemned "the continuation of Israeli military actions" and warned that "the unlawful occupation of our land beyond the 1974 line is a direct threat to the security of the region."
He demanded an "immediate and unconditional withdrawal."
But last week Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said that his country planned to keep troops in Syria.
Israel captured most of the Golan from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, in a move not recognized by most of the international community.
The incursions have been condemned by the United Nations chief as "violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
Despite tensions between the neighbors, Israel and Syria's new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks and have agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in June denied that his country sought to intervene militarily in Lebanon, where Israel is raising a separate war, after U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Damascus could get involved.
Hezbollah fought alongside Assad in the country's civil war, making al-Sharaa and the new authorities who toppled the former leader in 2024 deeply hostile to the group.
Syria's war shattered the country's infrastructure and pushed millions of people to flee internally and abroad.

articles.title: Russia may introduce covert coercive measures instead of mobilization – CCD
articles.body:
Russia may introduce covert coercive measures instead of mobilization – CCD
Andrii Kovalenko, head of the Center for Countering Disinformation at Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, said this in a Telegram post, Ukrinform reports.
"A number of economists in Russia and some political elites continue to advise Putin against announcing mobilization. Closed-door polling conducted weekly by Putin's administration across the regions also indicates a lack of public support for such a move. Instead, the possibility of covert coercive measures to increase the share of people signing contracts is being considered," he said.
According to Kovalenko, Putin wants mobilization, but carrying it out could undermine the existing social contract between the Russian authorities and the population. The war is generally perceived as something distant from most Russians, while participation in it is associated with financial compensation.
"Simply put, it is life in exchange for money. Mobilization would destroy this arrangement," Kovalenko said.
At the same time, he said Putin does not plan to end the war at least until 2028 and is already drawing up plans for military operations throughout 2027. However, not everyone supports these ambitions, meaning there is still room to influence Moscow.
"There are tools to exert such influence – our strikes on the Russian economy, EU support, all multiplied by the will of the United States and China," Kovalenko said.
He noted that this room for influence is limited but not hopeless. At the same time, he said, it is important for Ukraine to maintain internal unity, as Russia will devote significant resources not only to the battlefield but also to the information and political spheres.
"They will support certain potential political [projects] in Ukraine, bringing money into the country and looking for leaders. This track has not gone away," Kovalenko concluded.
Photo: Center for Countering Disinformation

articles.title: Pentagon demands audit of 30 universities, investigating Russian, Chinese, Iranian research ties
articles.body:
The US Defense Department formally notified 30 domestic academic institutions, directing them to immediately review their "academic, financial, and research collaborations with foreign entities of concern," the department announced on Monday.
The "foreign entities of concern" are defined as institutions listed under Section 1286 of the Fiscal Year 2019 National Defense Authorization Act, "as well as organizations associated with the rebranded Confucius Institutes," the Defense Department said.
The list includes 130 research institutes based in Russia, China, and Iran, including civilian universities.
The 30 US universities must "complete a comprehensive audit of all identified foreign collaborations, assess the exposure of sensitive or export-controlled research, and implement strict mitigation plans, including the termination of problematic partnerships," the department said. All findings must be submitted to the Defense Department by August 31, it said.
The department did not publicly name the 30 institutions. However, a US official listed the institutions to Fox News.
US universities under review includes Harvard, UC Berkeley, MIT, NYU, official tells FOX News
According to the official, the institutions are: Georgetown University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of California, Berkeley, University of California, San Diego, University of Texas at Austin, Emory University, Harvard University, Oklahoma State University, Penn State University, University of California, Los Angeles, University of Cincinnati, University of Minnesota, University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, University of South Carolina, University of Southern California, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bryant University, Cornell University, Drake University, Duke University, Illinois Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, New York University, Northeastern State University, Tahlequah (Oklahoma), Portland State University, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale, Stony Brook University, University of Delaware, and University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign.
The department is making its efforts alongside "partners in Congress," including the "House and Senate Armed Services Committees, the House and Senate Appropriations Committees, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party," it noted.
This coordination allows the Defense Department to "continue to build a robust research ecosystem that protects critical discoveries from exploitation," it added.
"This action is designed to protect American taxpayer-funded research investments from unauthorized technology transfer, intellectual property theft, and adversarial exploitation," the department said.
"The Department of War has zero tolerance for academic partnerships that compromise our national security," Undersecretary of War for Research and Engineering, Emil Michael, said.
"Institutions that receive funding from American taxpayers must uphold the highest standards of research security, and these mandated audits will ensure accountability across the board," Michael added.
"Universities are critical partners in executing a wide range of Department of War research programs, and the Department must therefore ensure that our research investments are well protected from foreign exploitation," Assistant Secretary of War for Science and Technology, Dr. Joseph Jewell, said.
Since the start of fiscal year 2026, the Pentagon cannot fund "fundamental research" with any organization on the list. Under the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, the Trump administration downgraded China to the US's second-ranked threat.
However, this recent clampdown comes amid ongoing intensity in the Pentagon's scrutiny of how China can use American research and technology to improve its military capabilities.
This includes a review of how China's military researchers used outputs from US artificial intelligence models to train domestic systems, published by Reuters in June.
US repeatedly investigating Harvard for ties to Chinese research, academics
Additionally, an investigation into Harvard University, which is one of the institutions named by the US official to FOX News, stated that Harvard failed to safeguard research collaborations with Chinese institutions, according to FOX.
The Ivy League school also allegedly received over $600m. from China under the federal Section 117 foreign-gift disclosure system, FOX reported. This would constitute more than any other US university, according to an Education Department dashboard cited in a report from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
Further, Harvard-affiliated researchers allegedly co-wrote work with academics from China's National University of Defense Technology, Beihang University, and Nanjing University of Science and Technology, as well as other Chinese institutions that are tied to the Chinese military, according to an investigation led by the Republican Party.
The investigation, reported by the South China Morning Post, a Hong Kong-based English-language outlet whose website is blocked in mainland China, cited the investigation, adding that the Republican Party's findings also accused Harvard of lacking the centralized infrastructure needed to identify and vet foreign research partnerships.

articles.title: Israel strikes Syrian military airfield after Turkish delegation visit, drawing rare US rebuke
articles.body:
Israel carried out an unusual strike deep inside Syria overnight, targeting the Abu al-Duhur military airfield in the eastern Idlib countryside after a reported visit by a Turkish military delegation to the site, according to Syrian and regional reports. The attack prompted rare public criticism from U.S. special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack, who said he was “deeply concerned” and described the strikes as an “unnecessary escalation.”
Syrian military officials told Reuters that four unidentified aircraft struck the airfield, damaging runways and storage facilities. One military official and a resident living nearby said there were no fatalities. The Sabereen News agency also reported that a runway at the base had been hit.
Syrian authorities blamed Israel for the attack, which came after a prolonged period without reported IDF strikes deep inside the country. The IDF declined to comment on the reports, but a senior Israeli official later acknowledged to Fox News that Israel had carried out the operation.
The official said Jerusalem had shared “sensitive intelligence” with Washington before the strike and that the information had been passed “at the highest levels of the various agencies and bodies” in both countries.
The official also sent a message to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, saying: “He understands that he cannot operate like the previous Syrian regime. It is possible that he did not understand what was happening, or did not know.”
Barrack, however, issued an unusually pointed condemnation. In a post, he said the “confirmed” strikes represented “an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability.”
He praised al-Sharaa’s government, saying Syria under his leadership “has not adopted an aggressive posture and has not maintained proxy forces.” Instead, Barrack said, Damascus had repeatedly expressed a preference for reducing tensions with Israel.
“The United States continues to believe that restraint and diplomatic engagement are the more constructive path,” he said. “We encourage all parties to prioritize reasonable dialogue over further military incidents.”
Turkey also strongly condemned the Israeli strikes on Abu al-Duhur air base, accusing Israel of violating international law and urging a tougher international response. “We call on the international community to take a more decisive stance to end Israel’s escalating aggression against Syria,” the Turkish Foreign Ministry said Tuesday.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani also accused Israel of responsibility during a joint press conference with International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi.
“We condemn the Israeli aggression, which constitutes an unjustified provocation, a violation of Syrian sovereignty and a direct threat to regional and international stability,” al-Shaibani said.
The two officials reaffirmed what they described as Syria’s sovereignty and called for an immediate end to Israeli violations. Syrian officials said Damascus was committed to becoming “a pillar of stability at the regional and international level,” while accusing Israel of pursuing a policy of “aggression and chaos.”
The Syrian Foreign Ministry later issued a separate statement explicitly blaming Israel. “Syria strongly condemns the Israeli airstrikes against Abu al-Duhur airport in Idlib province,” it said, calling the attack “unjustified aggression, a violation of Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region.”
The ministry said it held Israel responsible for the escalation and called on the international community and the UN Security Council to condemn the strike.
Sources cited by the Qatari outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed said the Israeli attack came after a Turkish military delegation visited Abu al-Duhur to examine rehabilitation of its runway. That timing could add another layer of sensitivity to the strike amid Turkey’s growing role in postwar Syria.
Abu al-Duhur airfield lies about 27 kilometers east of Saraqib, near the village of Abu al-Duhur. Its position between the provinces of Idlib, Hama and Aleppo, close to the Syrian desert, has long given it strategic significance.
The base was considered one of northern Syria’s more prominent military installations under the previous regime. Estimates of its size vary, with some sources placing it at roughly 16 square kilometers and others at about 23 square kilometers. The facility includes several runways.
During the Syrian civil war, opposition forces captured the airfield in 2015. Forces loyal to the former Syrian regime retook it in January 2018 following a major offensive launched in late 2017 with Russian support.
The overnight attack stands out because of both its location and the diplomatic reaction it triggered. While Israel has repeatedly acted inside Syria over the years against what it described as military threats, the strike drew an unusually direct rebuke from Washington at a time when the U.S. administration is publicly urging restraint and diplomatic engagement between Jerusalem and Damascus.

articles.title: Jason Arday’s death and the racist weaponisation of plagiarism
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Jason Arday’s death and the racist weaponisation of plagiarism
On 18 July 2003, the body of UK weapons scientist Dr. David Kelly was discovered in the woods of Oxfordshire, some twenty miles away from the library where I was then writing a doctorate about Iraq. His death was ruled a suicide.
23 years later, Dr Jason Arday was found dead in south London, a few days after resigning from the University of Cambridge over allegations that he copied another person’s thesis, including the typographical errors.
Both Kelly and Arday were named, pushed into the media spotlight, and destroyed.
I never met Kelly, but we sat in the same seat a few days apart during a UK parliamentary inquiry. I was summoned to Parliament in 2003 because the British government had plagiarised material from my thesis and copied it into a dossier that Colin Powell presented to the United Nations to justify the invasion of Iraq, including my typographical errors.
Ironically, I was an Anglo-American of Iraqi heritage whose research had inadvertently become part of the justification for the invasion of my ancestral homeland. I never needed convincing that plagiarism matters. Since 2003, I have been trying to convince public audiences that it does.
In my Newlines Magazine article, ‘From the Dodgy Dossier to the Cambridge Controversies, Not All Plagiarism Is Alike,’ I wrote about the 2023 case in which Claudine Gay, the first Black president of Harvard University in Cambridge, US, was the target of plagiarism allegations. In Cambridge, UK, Jason Arday was the youngest Black professor in the university’s history. While my work was linked to the Iraq War, they were targets in the culture war over Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI).
Plagiarism is a matter to be weaponised, and only the strong have the power to survive its attack. Rarely do those caught up in plagiarism cases survive the attack.
Nobody in Tony Blair’s government, as far as we know, was disciplined for the plagiarism, despite lengthy trials and testimonies, including the Hutton Inquiry. The UK government taught a lesson that plagiarism is survivable if you have power. The lesson from Gay and Arday’s death is that it is not survivable without power.
In Arday’s case, there is another connection to those without power. It is rarely asked if his neurodivergence was a factor in what played out, similar to the life of the mathematician John Nash, the Nobel Prize winner whose struggle with mental illness inspired the movie “A Beautiful Mind.”
In all three cases, plagiarism led to three academics leaving their university positions.
In my TEDx IE Madrid talk ‘The Dodgy Dossier, the Iraq War, and Me,’ I talk about how when I moved to Istanbul, Turkey, to take my first academic job in 2004, Turkish newspapers featured headlines tying me to the justification for the 2003 war, with some headlines calling me its architect or “mastermind.” Taxi drivers and fruit vendors asked me why I had started it.
At my university, leftist students organised protests against my presence and called me the architect of the Iraq War. In this case, it was weaponised by leftist students opposed to the Iraq War. Tragically, I agreed with them and told them so directly when they confronted me.
I had not plagiarised anyone, but rather I was the person plagiarised from, by a government whose war I opposed, using work I had written to explain to Saddam Hussein’s police state, which I also opposed. None of that mattered. Like the professors who followed me, a crowd decided my name did not belong in a lecture hall. They were not interested in learning the difference between the man who did the research and the government that stole it.
They have good reason to. As for the death of Dr. Kelly, this is how I most likely became a target in Turkey.
Another UK government report, issued in September 2002, falsely claimed that Iraq could deploy chemical munitions in 45 minutes. Kelly, a scientist in the UK Ministry of Defence and a commentator on a draft of that dossier, revealed to the BBC that the 45-minute figure was an exaggeration and asserted that Alistair Campbell, Blair’s media advisor, used that figure to “sex-up” the Iraqi WMD threat, giving the September 2002 dossier the title the “sexed-up dossier.”
My work was plagiarised in a February 2003 dossier known as the “dodgy dossier,” for which Campbell also took responsibility.
It was during the media frenzy in the UK that Kelly died by suicide. The dossiers became interchangeable in media reporting, and I argue they could collectively be labelled the “dodgy sex dossier.”
Those who did not follow the affair closely, including the Turkish media and students, associated me with the 45-minute claim. This conflation unleashed hostility toward me both in my personal and public lives, but nothing like that endured by Gay and Arday, who faced death threats and a barrage of racist tirades.
This precedent demonstrates that, over time, the nuances in these cases will be forgotten, with juries already having made up their minds.
I do not compare my life to the deaths of Arday or Kelly, or Gay’s resignation. My experience in Turkey led me to teach at IE University in Madrid and Segovia, which turned out to be a dynamic, cosmopolitan campus—a silver lining.
Yet all universities around the world need to have courses on plagiarism for both professors and students, especially in the age of artificial intelligence. The state universities in California where I work cite a lack of funding for these courses, but they have agreements with major AI and plagiarism tech companies. For years, I have approached these companies that make plagiarism software, telling them: “If you make money from selling this technology to universities, you can give back by teaching how to avoid plagiarism in the first place,” but to no avail.
Finally, bringing up the “dodgy dossier” should serve as a prominent reminder that civil society and the media need to remain vigilant. If the US and UK launched a war against Iraq in 2003 based on fabricated evidence, there should have been a greater uproar over the so-called intelligence that the US claimed to attack Iran in 2026.
Ibrahim Al-Marashi is an associate professor of Middle East history at California State University, on the board of the International Security and Conflict Resolution (ISCOR) program at San Diego State University, and a visiting faculty member at The American College of the Mediterranean and the Department of International Relations at Central European University. His publications include Iraq’s Armed Forces: An Analytical History (2008), The Modern History of Iraq (2017), and A Concise History of the Middle East (2024).
Follow him on Twitter: @ialmarashi
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@alaraby.co.uk
