Erbil false-flag attack: Foreign sabotage against Iran-Iraq unity
TEHRAN — The recent drone incident targeting the private office of Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) Prime Minister Masrour Barzani and the residence of the Security Directorate in Erbil represents a suspicious escalation designed to undermine fragile regional diplomacy. Occurring at a moment when Tehran and Iraqi authorities have made tangible progress on border security agreements, the timing and execution of these strikes point toward a calculated attempt by external actors to derail neighborly ties.
As Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi explicitly noted, nothing justifies the attack on PM Barzani’s office, cautioning that Kurdish partners must remain vigilant against false-flag ploys engineered to sow discord between neighbors. Several analytical factors support the assessment that this operation was staged by hostile third parties. Tehran has consistently prioritized stable, constructive relations with Baghdad and Erbil, meaning an unprovoked attack against top KRG executive offices yields zero strategic benefit for Iran while completely undermining diplomatic goodwill. Furthermore, launching drone assets near border vectors serves as a classic false-flag signature, engineered to prompt immediate public blame before independent investigative committees can establish true launch origins or actor identities.
With US and Israeli military initiatives encountering severe strategic bottlenecks in their broader pressure campaign against Iran, orchestrating internal regional friction serves direct operational objectives for Washington and Tel Aviv. Creating a sudden security crisis in Iraqi Kurdistan provides a high-visibility operational distraction, effectively shifting focus away from strategic setbacks elsewhere in the theater. Moreover, reported efforts by Western intelligence agencies and foreign officials to mobilize anti-Iranian militia factions indicate an active strategy to weaponize northern Iraq. By staging a provocative attack and framing Tehran, foreign intelligence operators seek to ignite anti-Iranian sentiment in Erbil, constructing a public pretext to supply air cover, advanced weaponry, and logistics to separatist militias operating along Iran’s western frontier.
Ultimately, the investigative committee established by Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi must rigorously examine technical signatures and foreign intelligence footprints rather than relying on surface-level assumptions. Erbil and Tehran share a vital imperative to resist external manipulation, disarm destabilizing armed groups, and ensure foreign covert operations cannot subvert regional sovereignty or compromise neighborly stability.

articles.title: Kushner's visit to Netanyahu deepens Gaza's frustration on deal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Kushner's visit to Netanyahu deepens Gaza's frustration over deadlocked talks
The lengthy meeting between US envoy Jared Kushner and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday has deepened frustration in Gaza, where Palestinians see negotiations over the ceasefire's next phase as trapped in a cycle of disputes over Hamas's weapons, Israeli withdrawal and promises of reconstruction.
The meeting lasted about eight hours and included Israeli officials and representatives of the so-called "Board of Peace", Israeli media outlets reported.
Netanyahu's office claimed in a press statement that the talks ended with an agreement to establish two working groups, one focusing on the disarmament of Gaza and another on sanitation, water and public health.
While Netanyahu's office described the discussions as "constructive and in-depth", many Palestinians saw little to suggest that the meeting would resolve the issues preventing the transition to the next phase of the supposed ceasefire.
Kushner met a Hamas delegation in Cairo before traveling to Israel. He said Hamas leaders "said all the right things" but emphasised Washington would judge them by their actions, not words.
He said disarmament progress could start in 30 days, with the US aiming for weapon removal and tunnel destruction in 60-90 days. Washington will not allow Gaza to rebuild until disarmament is done, but Israel retains the right to self-defence against perceived threats.
For Gaza residents, such timelines are disconnected from the daily reality of displacement, destroyed homes and shortages of basic necessities.
Reconstruction remains hostage
The central concern for many Palestinians is no longer how Hamas's weapons will be handled, but whether the political process can deliver a permanent end to Israel's violence, remove an Israeli occupation, and begin meaningful reconstruction.
"Kushner's meeting with Netanyahu offered little hope to families still struggling to survive," Radi Abu Afash, a father of six from Gaza City, told The New Arab.
"People in Gaza want to see results on the ground, not another series of statements and promises," he said, adding that his priority was for his children to live safely and have access to food, water and healthcare.
Abu Afash said that Palestinians were following the negotiations with concern because Israeli demands appeared to be dominating the process, while the needs of Gaza's population were pushed aside.
Salah Abu Hasira, who lives in a tent on Gaza City's beach after losing all his brothers and three of his sons, told TNA that the political discussions had become increasingly disconnected from the reality facing Palestinians.
His family, he said, had already paid an enormous price during the war. Any political initiative would mean little unless it brought a tangible improvement to people's lives.
"What Palestinians need now is an end to their suffering, dignified shelter, rebuilt homes and a future for children who have lost their parents and relatives," he added.
He said that the absence of Palestinian voices from high-level discussions reinforced the feeling that decisions about Gaza's future were being made without its residents.
For Samira Ayoub, also from Gaza City, the political debate comes amid the burden of caring for around 15 grandchildren after losing four of her children during the war.
Ayoub told TNA that the loss of her children had transformed her life, leaving her responsible for her grandchildren while living through extremely difficult conditions.
"Gaza's families can no longer endure more waiting," she said. "People who have lost their children, homes and livelihoods need concrete steps to restore security and stability."
"Palestinians wanted more than an agreement on paper: they wanted children to return to school, families to secure food and water, and survivors to rebuild their lives," she added.
A wider crisis
Frustration has grown with each new round of meetings that produces fresh working groups and deadlines without visible changes in Gaza.
Taysir Abdullah, a Gaza-based political analyst, told TNA that the expectations that Hamas would surrender its weapons completely and immediately were unrealistic.
He argued that Hamas could manoeuvre, delay, and adjust its positions but unlikely to take a step that could undermine its political and organisational existence. As an ideological movement deriving strength from its resistance identity, publicly surrendering its weapons could be seen as an admission of defeat.
Abdullah said Hamas might accept a gradual disarmament if conditions protect its political and symbolic standing, such as avoiding footage of weapons handovers, extending the process, and using a non-Israeli or non-American mediator.
He believes Hamas is relying partly on time, Turkish and Qatari political support and possible changes in Israel's political landscape, particularly ahead of elections.
Mustafa Ibrahim, another political analyst, takes a more pessimistic view. He describes the current proposals as "cosmetic concessions" that could restore aspects of daily life in Gaza without addressing the underlying political crisis.
Allowing limited sanitation, water and infrastructure projects, Ibrahim says, could reflect Israel's concern over the humanitarian and health consequences of Gaza's devastation rather than a genuine move towards ending the blockade or occupation.
"The danger is that these concessions become a substitute for a political solution," he added, warning against treating Gaza merely as a humanitarian, health and security problem requiring containment.
Political analyst Esmat Mansour, meanwhile, believes Hamas's acceptance of a disarmament process, regardless of how it is ultimately implemented, represents a significant strategic shift.
He argues that Hamas's adherence to the agreement could serve its interests as the confrontation moves from the military arena to the political and diplomatic one.
With Palestinians lacking sufficient leverage to impose their demands by force, Mansour believes the movement must rely on Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, the United States and international pressure to push Israel towards implementing the agreement.
Israel blocks next phase
Amid the uncertainty, Palestinian factions met in Cairo on Monday, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the Democratic Reform Movement.
Hamas said its political bureau chief, Khalil al-Hayya, briefed the factions on meetings with Egyptian officials, mediators and guarantors in El Alamein, as well as subsequent discussions on the roadmap for the second phase of the ceasefire agreement.
The factions noted Israel was obstructing the transition to the second phase, accusing the government of reneging on understandings reached during the first phase and continuing violations.
They also discussed efforts to halt what they described as escalating aggression and prevent Gaza from becoming a casualty of Israel's political and electoral struggles, while accelerating relief, recovery and reconstruction.
Israeli media, citing political sources, reported that Netanyahu insisted during his meeting with Kushner on maintaining the Israeli army's freedom of action in Gaza. The meeting reportedly included the Shin Bet chief and the head of Military Intelligence, who presented what Israel described as evidence of Hamas violations.
Trump, meanwhile, said it would be better if Israel did not attack Gaza again, remarks welcomed by Hamas, which urged the US president to pressure the Israeli government to honour the understandings reached for the second phase.
For Palestinians, however, the contradiction remains stark: Washington is pressing for progress while Israel continues to insist on security conditions and freedom of military action.

Shares fall in Asia, with Kospi down 5.2%, while oil prices jump
BANGKOK (AP) — Shares slipped Wednesday in Asia after Wall Street pulled further from its all-time high as artificial-intelligence stocks resumed their decline.
South Korea’s Kospi led the regional retreat, dropping 5.2% to 6,515.97. The two biggest companies benefiting from the AI boom tracked losses for their U.S. rivals. Samsung Electronics shed 6.9%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix tumbled 7.9%.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 sank 2.6% to 65,703.78. The Hang Seng in Hong Kong lost 0.4% to 25,382.66, while the Shanghai Composite index shed 1.5% to 3,927.70. Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1.4%, and Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4% to 9,083.70.
Apart from renewed jitters over criticism that AI-related stocks have shot too high, rising oil prices also were clouding market sentiment.
Crude prices have been swinging sharply due to uncertainty about when and whether the United States and Iran can reach a deal to allow oil tankers to exit the Persian Gulf freely again. Brent was going for $72.87 per barrel just before the start of the war.
Brent crude, the international standard, surged 0.9% to $91.83 per barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil gained 1% to $84.88 per barrel
On Tuesday, Wall Street pulled further from its all-time high. The S&P 500 fell 0.7% for a third straight modest loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 0.2%, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1.3%.
Stocks that have been big winners in the boom around AI technology led the decline. They’ve been veering up and down this summer on worries that their prices have shot too high and that the strong demand for memory, processors and other building blocks of data centers may fizzle if AI proves less profitable than promised.
Micron Technology dropped 7%, and the seller of computer memory was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500. So were chip companies Nvidia, which fell 2.3%, and Broadcom, which sank 3.2%.
Even with their recent swings, such stocks remain big winners, and Micron has more than tripled this year.
Bond yields have been another concern. They have jumped since the war began because high oil prices are pushing inflation higher. That adds to worries over huge debt loads for governments, while surging borrowing keeps yields high.
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury edged down to 4.70% from 4.72% late Monday but remains well above its 3.97% level from just before the war with Iran began. The 30-year Treasury yield also ticked lower but is still near its highest level since 2007.
When bond yields are high, investors are less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other kinds of investments, particularly those seen as the most expensive.
High yields have already sent the average long-term U.S. mortgage rate near its highest level in a year, which has hurt the housing industry. A report on Tuesday said homebuilders broke ground on fewer new houses last month than economists expected.
High yields could also slow borrowing by Big Tech companies to pay for data centers, threatening a big source of growth for the U.S. economy.
In other dealings early Wednesday, the U.S. dollar fell to 159.37 Japanese yen from 159.59 yen. The euro rose to $1.1582 from $1.1574.

AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump abandons ‘hammer Iran ASAP’ approach – CNN
articles.body:
Trump abandons ‘hammer Iran ASAP’ approach – CNN
The US has suspended negotiations with Iran and is seeking to gradually “strangle” the country, CNN reported on Tuesday, after its bombing campaign near the Strait of Hormuz failed to yield the desired results.
The US abruptly halted its most recent wave of strikes late last month amid reports that the war, launched alongside Israel on February 28, has largely depleted its stockpiles of precision munitions and interceptor missiles. US top brass have also reportedly warned President Donald Trump that the military has exhausted its list of targets near the Strait of Hormuz.
White House officials reportedly told political allies that they were changing strategy in what a CNN source described as “going from ‘hammer Iran ASAP’ to ‘strangle them’ over time.”
According to the outlet, Trump instructed his negotiators, including Vice President J.D. Vance and envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to halt talks with Tehran.
“There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday, adding that the US blockade of Iranian ports remained “in full force and effect.”
The June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU), which provided a 60-day window to negotiate a definitive peace deal between the US and Iran, expired on Monday as the two sides clashed over its interpretation. Iran’s key negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, last week denounced what he called “theater diplomacy,” accusing the US of issuing unacceptable ultimatums.
Ghalibaf said on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US lifts its blockade, releases Iran’s frozen assets, and removes sanctions. Iran closed the strategic waterway, which handles around a quarter of global seaborne oil and LNG trade, shortly after the US and Israel launched their bombing campaign in late February. The US Navy declared its own blockade in April and has since been guiding ships through routes that Iran considers illegal.

articles.title: Ukraine vows to respond after Russian strike kills 10 in northeast region
articles.body:
Ukraine vows to respond after Russian strike kills 10 in northeast region
Officials say the rocket strike on Pechenihy, a village about 40km from the Russian border, hit a busy intersection and 17 others were wounded
A Russian attack on a village in the Kharkiv region of northeast Ukraine killed 10 people, Kyiv said on Tuesday, vowing to respond.
The strike comes amid a surge in civilian deaths in the four-and-a-half-year war.
Russian forces “carried out a rocket strike on Pechenihy”, a village around 40km (25 miles) from the Russian border, Kharkiv regional governor Oleg Synegubov said on social media.
“According to preliminary information, 10 people were killed,” he added, with 17 people wounded.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on social media that the strike hit a busy intersection, “a location with a post office and stores, surrounded only by residential buildings”.
Images from the site of the attack posted by the Ukrainian emergency services showed rescuers working at the scene, carrying people to safety amid destroyed buildings, smouldering rubble and cars on fire or reduced to charred shells.

articles.title: Israeli military patrol approaches Syrian town southwest of Damascus: Local media
articles.body:
Laith Al-Jnaidi and Mohammad Sio
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
An Israeli military patrol on Tuesday entered the outskirts of Syria’s town of Beit Jinn located southwest of Damascus, local media has reported.
According to Syria’s Alikhbariah television channel, the patrol has approached Bat al-Warda, a hill overlooking Beit Jinn.
The channel did not provide details on the size of the Israeli force or the ostensible aim of the incursion.
The reported incident comes amid repeated Israeli attacks and armed incursions in southwestern Syria, especially areas west of Damascus.
Syrian authorities have yet to comment on the latest incident, while Israel has not publicly explained why its forces reportedly entered the area.
The reported incursion comes shortly after Israeli warplanes struck the Abu al-Duhur Military Airbase in Syria’s northwestern Idlib province.
Before the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in late 2024, Israel frequently struck positions in Syria that it claimed were linked to Iranian-backed forces.
Following al-Assad’s ouster, Israel expanded its strikes to include weapons depots and strategic military positions throughout Syria.
In recent weeks, southwestern Syria has seen almost daily Israeli attacks and incursions, which have included raids, searches, arrest campaigns, and the setting up of military checkpoints.
In late July, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said his government was working in tandem with several countries to conclude a security agreement with Israel.
He said a successful agreement would “pave the way for comprehensive peace” without abandoning Syria’s claim to the Golan Heights, most of which Israel has occupied since 1967.
Following al-Assad’s departure, Israel declared its 1974 Disengagement Agreement with Syria null and void before seizing a UN-monitored buffer zone and other positions inside Syrian territory.

articles.title: 450 fictitious mobilizations uncovered in three regions through manipulation of the "Oberih" register — Prosecutor General's Office
articles.body:
450 fictitious mobilizations uncovered in three regions through manipulation of the "Oberih" register — Prosecutor General's Office
Kyiv • UNN
Recruitment and Social Support Center officials in Zakarpattia, Ternopil region and Bukovyna entered false data into the "Oberih" register, inflating conscription figures. The fictitious entries included active-duty military personnel, a deceased person and a prisoner of war.
Employees of the specialized prosecutor's offices in the defense sector of the Western Region, together with law enforcement officers, uncovered large-scale manipulation of mobilization data in three regions in western Ukraine. The regions in question are Zakarpattia, Ternopil and Chernivtsi, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
The investigation established that officials of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in the three aforementioned regions entered false information into the "Oberih" registry about allegedly mobilized citizens, thereby artificially inflating the indicators for fulfilling mobilization targets.
To enter the false information, the suspects used their own qualified electronic signatures and official access to the "Oberih" registry. They entered data on people who had not actually been drafted, including serving military personnel, a deceased serviceman, and a serviceman who is being held captive in Russia
In Chernivtsi region, a 35-year-old former head of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers entered false information into the registry about the mobilization of 99 people, using, among other things, fabricated personal details.
In Ternopil region, a 39-year-old former head of a district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center registered another 18 people as allegedly mobilized.
In Zakarpattia, a 36-year-old former deputy head of a district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center organized a group consisting of the center's managers and operators.
They entered data on already mobilized citizens into "Oberih," registering them as allegedly undergoing a second military medical examination and a new draft. In this way, 329 fictitious mobilizations were registered
The suspects' actions were qualified under Parts 1 and 3 of Article 362, Part 1 of Article 366, Part 3 of Article 27, Part 3 of Article 28, and Part 5 of Article 27 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, depending on each person's role. The charges concern official forgery, the commission of a criminal offense by a group of persons, complicity in a criminal offense, as well as unauthorized actions involving information processed in electronic computing machines and automated systems. The suspects face lengthy imprisonment.
Recall
Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko reported that ten servicemen from one of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in Odesa had been served with notices of suspicion. They are suspected of unlawfully depriving people of their liberty and torturing them. At least eight victims have been identified.

articles.title: Air Force Wants New Family of Target Drones Ranging from Expendable to Sophisticated
articles.body:
The Air Force is looking for a new family of drones to serve as aerial targets for test missions, ranging from cheap, expendable quadcopters to large, reusable aircraft that can mimic fifth-generation enemy fighters.
The service’s Aerial Targets Program Office published a request for information on Aug. 14 asking the defense industry for ideas for a “family of systems needed throughout the spectrum of missions in Defensive and Offensive Counter Air capabilities” to provide realistic aerial targets for Air Force munitions and missile programs during validation testing prior to full-rate production.
The Air Force wants interested firms to submit ideas to satisfy any of three tiers of unmanned aerial targets:
- Tier One: High-end, reusable targets capable of emulating “modern threat” fighter aircraft capable of flying from Mach .9 to supersonic speeds and withstanding maneuvers between five and nine Gs.
- Tier Two: Reusable but expendable Group 3 and 4 drones similar to the size of an MQ-1 Predator. Systems should be capable of speeds between Mach .5 and.8 and withstanding maneuvers between six and eight Gs. Designs should feature a low-cost construction permitting a service life of up to 10 flights.
- Tier Three: Low-cost, Group 1 and 2 drones weighing up to 55 pounds. These targets should be capable of flying at speeds of up to 172 miles per hour and designed to be “to be shot down in high volumes during air defense and close-in weapon system” training.
The Air Force currently uses systems such as the BQM-167A unmanned aerial target and threat simulator for weapons development, testing, and training. The system can represent air targets maneuvering at up to 9 Gs at speeds up to Mach 0.91.
“As operational environments evolve, there is increasing demand for” capabilities such as “lower-cost, scalable target systems, flexible and rapidly deployable solutions” as well as systems that can be treated as expendable when required,” the notice states.
Interested firms have until Sept. 28 to respond to the solicitation. “The objective is to identify a diverse range of options capable of satisfying the specified performance requirements, as these target solutions will be tested in live fire settings,” the RFI states.
Where practical, systems should be capable of safe and efficient launch and recovery operations. Launch options may include standard runway operations as well as ground-based assisted or rail launch systems, th states. Recovery options for Tier One and Two designs should include runway landings or parachute recovery and minimize damage and reconstitution time wherever possible, the notice stated.
“Proposed solutions should demonstrate threat-representative aerial target capabilities and flexible performance characteristics,” the solicitation states. “Submissions should detail compatibility with existing or adaptable control systems, such as the Air Force’s Advanced Airborne Threat Target Control System (AATTCS) or satellite communications-capable.”
If incompatible with AATTCS, “submitters should provide the capabilities and associated costs of maintaining their alternative control system,” according to the RFI. “Physical platforms should have on-board aerial target flight termination resources that ensure required range safety” such as “aircraft destruct” mode or a “thrust control neutralization” feature.
Interested firms should describe the “maturity of their system’s design and any existing modeling, simulation, or flight test data that validates performance claims,” according to the RFI.
The aerial target RFI is the latest Air Force move to scour the defense industry for ways to use drones to solve future battlefield challenges. In an Aug. 7 request for information, the service’s Rapid Sustainment Office asked industry to submit ideas for creating a drone factory in a box—expeditionary manufacturing equipment for producing and maintaining Group 1 and 2 drones for reconnaissance, attack, and counter-drone missions.
